contents.title: Reading: The audit that changed how a team judged its own decision
contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about past modality: obligation, deduction & regret require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
Within a charity reviewing an emergency purchase made during a supply shortage, a seemingly straightforward question became an exercise in judgment rather than procedure. The central responsibility belonged to the finance chair, Mariam Latif. The decision was whether the purchasing team had acted irresponsibly by ordering more equipment than was eventually used. The issue mattered because an early decision would shape what colleagues, stakeholders, and later reviewers treated as the working interpretation. A premature conclusion could create momentum that was difficult to reverse, while excessive caution could delay a useful response. The group therefore treated the wording of the decision as part of the decision itself: what it said needed to reflect not only preference, but what the available information could actually support. Two strands of evidence carried most weight. First, at the time of purchase, suppliers had warned that replacement stock might not arrive for six weeks. Second, the shortage eased unexpectedly after another organization released surplus equipment. Their convergence made it difficult to dismiss the issue as a one-off impression, yet the group resisted the easy leap from consistency to certainty. The strands did not necessarily measure the same construct, and neither automatically established a single causal explanation. Their real value lay in the pattern they formed and in the sharper questions that pattern allowed reviewers to ask. The main caveat was substantial: reviewers now knew the final outcome, but the purchasing team had not had that information when the decision was made. A limitation of this kind does not necessarily invalidate the underlying evidence; it changes what the evidence is entitled to support. The reviewers therefore replaced the crude question ‘Is the evidence good or bad?’ with a more useful one: ‘What is this evidence good enough to show?’ That distinction matters whenever a reliable dataset is narrow, a credible witness has only partial access, or a coherent model remains sensitive to assumptions that are open to challenge. A credible counter-position also had to be represented: one board member argued that the team need not have ordered so much because much of it remained unused. The group did not include this view as a ceremonial concession before returning to its preferred answer. Members tested whether the objection changed the interpretation of the evidence, the cost of acting, or the cost of waiting. In several parts of the discussion, the counterargument narrowed the wording and sharpened the conditions attached to the recommendation. That made the final position more defensible because the strongest alternative explanation had been answered rather than caricatured. The practical outcome was measured rather than dramatic: the audit concluded that the quantity may have been conservative but was defensible given the evidence available at the time. Just as important, the decision contained a theory of revision. If later evidence challenged the assumptions, the organization would have a defined reason to reconsider instead of defending the earlier position merely for consistency. Colleagues could also see which part of the conclusion rested on direct evidence, which part was inferential, and which part represented a judgment about acceptable risk. That transparency reduced the chance that a cautious claim would later be remembered as a categorical promise. The wider lesson is that past modals distinguish criticism, unnecessary action, possibility, and deduction; they should not collapse hindsight into certainty. Language contributes directly to that discipline. A reporting verb can imply endorsement or distance; a conditional can distinguish a real possibility from a remote hypothetical; a focusing structure can correct a mistaken assumption; and a nominal phrase can either package a familiar concept efficiently or conceal the agent who acted. Complexity is therefore not the goal. The relevant question is which formulation makes the logic, stance, and information structure most accurate for the audience and genre. For anyone facing a similar problem, the practical task is judging a past decision fairly when later information makes another choice look obvious. A strong response keeps the distinctions that matter, acknowledges uncertainty without becoming evasive, and remains readable enough for another person to act on. The result is not merely a more advanced piece of English. It is a better record of how a decision was reached and what would justify changing it.

| unfulfilled obligation | التزام لم يُنفّذ | The unit uses “unfulfilled obligation” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| unnecessary action | فعل غير ضروري | The unit uses “unnecessary action” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |

2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

## Answers

2. at the time of purchase, suppliers had warned that replacement stock might not arrive for six weeks
3. the shortage eased unexpectedly after another organization released surplus equipment
4. reviewers now knew the final outcome, but the purchasing team had not had that information when the decision was made
5. one board member argued that the team need not have ordered so much because much of it remained unused
6. the audit concluded that the quantity may have been conservative but was defensible given the evidence available at the time

contents.title: Listening: Did we really order too much?
contents.body:
## Before you listen
- Listen for how the speakers navigate complex arguments and counterarguments regarding past decisions, paying close attention to nuanced expressions of obligation and regret.
- Notice the sophisticated vocabulary and idiomatic expressions used to discuss evidence, responsibility, and the pitfalls of hindsight bias.

## Transcript
Omar: Well, Sara, this retrospective review of the procurement department's extravagant order of the new server racks has proven rather more contentious than I'd initially anticipated. The central question, of course, pivots on whether they really ought to have committed to such a substantial investment.

Sara: Precisely, Omar. It seems everyone's now an expert with the benefit of hindsight. But if we're to be truly objective, we must peel back the layers and assess what information they had at their disposal then. My contention, from what I've gleaned, is that they might well have been justified.

Omar: Justified? That's a bold claim, given the subsequent surplus. One could easily argue they needn't have placed such a colossal order. The storage facility is still groaning under the weight of unused units. What exactly, in your view, absolves them of what appears, prima facie, to be a miscalculation?

Sara: It boils down to the prevailing market intelligence. Suppliers, across the board, were forecasting a severe component shortage, a bottleneck that would inevitably impact lead times and pricing. The team was faced with a stark choice: procure aggressively or risk operational paralysis further down the line. They *couldn't have known* the supply chain would stabilise so abruptly.

Omar: That’s certainly a compelling counterpoint to the 'they should have known better' brigade. But there's the inevitable rejoinder: if they'd been more circumspect, perhaps they wouldn't have found themselves with such an embarrassing inventory overhang. We are, after all, talking about a substantial capital outlay that remains unproductive.

Sara: And herein lies the rub, doesn't it? The decision had to be made under conditions of significant uncertainty. Had they *not* ordered sufficiently, and the predicted shortage materialised, we'd now be lambasting them for a catastrophic failure of foresight. It’s a classic Catch-22, in a way. One truly *cannot* win.

Omar: Indeed. It's often the case that the road not taken appears, in retrospect, to have been the wiser path. But this isn't just an academic exercise. The board wants a definitive conclusion. Were they culpable, or were their actions a reasonable response to what *might have been*?

Sara: My position is that culpability is too strong a word. They were operating under considerable pressure, with credible threats to our operational continuity. They *must have felt* compelled to over-order as a protective measure. It wasn’t a matter of recklessness; it was risk mitigation.

Omar: So, your argument posits that what appears to be an error of judgment was, in fact, a calculated gamble that, through no fault of their own, didn't pay off in the anticipated manner? A nuanced distinction, to be sure.

Sara: Precisely. We shouldn't confuse outcome with intent. They *wouldn't have acted* so decisively if they hadn't genuinely believed it was necessary. The situation called for decisive action, and they provided it. The eventual glut was an unforeseen consequence of external market shifts, not internal misjudgment.

Omar: So, our recommendation then is to frame their actions as a defensible strategic choice given the available intelligence, rather than an egregious error they *should have avoided*? We must be careful not to whitewash the financial implications.

Sara: Absolutely. We acknowledge the financial cost, but we attribute it to external volatility, not an internal failing. We *could not have expected* them to possess a crystal ball. They acted in good faith, and that ought to count for something. It’s a tough lesson, but not one borne of negligence.

Omar: A sophisticated reframing indeed. So, the key takeaway is that while the outcome was sub-optimal, their decision-making process, considering the prevailing circumstances, *must be seen* as rational and prudent.

Sara: Exactly. We ought to learn from the incident, certainly, but not with a punitive lens. It’s a testament to the unpredictable nature of global supply chains, rather than an indictment of individual foresight. They *might well have been lauded* had the shortage materialised.

Omar: A salutary reminder that retrospective analysis, while essential, *must not be allowed* to morph into an unfair indictment. Let’s draft the report with that nuanced perspective.

Sara: Agreed. We must ensure the language reflects the complexity, ensuring we don't unduly castigate those who were genuinely trying to safeguard the company’s interests under duress. It’s an exercise in contextual empathy, really.

## Key phrases
- peeling back the layers
- found themselves with such an embarrassing inventory overhang
- herein lies the rub
- a catastrophic failure of foresight
- unduly castigate those who were genuinely trying to safeguard

## Comprehension
1. What contentious issue are Omar and Sara discussing regarding the procurement department?
2. What key factor does Sara believe might justify the procurement department's substantial order?
3. What common criticism does Omar acknowledge is often leveled against decisions that result in a surplus?
4. How does Sara reframe the procurement team's decision, differentiating it from mere misjudgment?
5. What overarching principle do Omar and Sara agree should guide the final report's conclusion?

## Answers
1. Whether the procurement department was justified in its extravagant order of server racks, given the subsequent surplus.
2. The prevailing market intelligence at the time, which forecast a severe component shortage, compelling the team to procure aggressively.
3. That the team "should have known better" and been more circumspect to avoid an embarrassing inventory overhang.
4. She argues it was a calculated gamble or risk mitigation strategy made under pressure and uncertainty, rather than recklessness, with the glut being an unforeseen consequence of external market shifts.
5. That retrospective analysis must not unfairly indict or castigate those who made rational, prudent decisions based on available information, even if the outcome was sub-optimal.

B: I would support this outcome: the audit concluded that the quantity may have been conservative but was defensible given the evidence available at the time. It gives us a decision without pretending the uncertainty has disappeared.

## Task 1

The strongest case for action is that at the time of purchase, suppliers had warned that replacement stock might not arrive for six weeks. In addition, the shortage eased unexpectedly after another organization released surplus equipment. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because reviewers now knew the final outcome, but the purchasing team had not had that information when the decision was made. A credible objection is that one board member argued that the team need not have ordered so much because much of it remained unused. contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about concession beyond although require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
The case developed within a university considering whether to extend evening access to specialist laboratories. Responsibility for the judgment rested with the academic planning committee. The decision concerned whether to approve a one-year evening-access pilot. None of the available positions was absurd, which was precisely why the discussion demanded care. Each option highlighted a different risk: acting too quickly, waiting too long, or communicating a degree of certainty that the evidence did not warrant. Instead of asking which position sounded most confident, participants separated what could be observed directly from what had to be inferred and from what depended on a value judgment about acceptable consequences. The evidential picture was stronger than a single headline figure suggested. One important observation was that student surveys showed strong demand among final-year researchers with daytime placements. Alongside it, two departments already had trained staff on site during part of the proposed evening period. That combination gave the discussion substance, but it also raised a methodological question: did the two observations independently support the same conclusion, or did they illuminate different parts of the problem? Treating them as interchangeable would have simplified the argument at the cost of accuracy. The review therefore kept their distinct functions visible while considering what they implied together. The most important constraint appeared when the group considered scope rather than direction: additional security, supervision, and insurance costs would be significant. This did not erase the positive findings, but it prevented them from carrying more weight than they could reasonably bear. The team distinguished uncertainty about whether an effect existed from uncertainty about its size, cause, duration, or transfer to another context. That separation made the discussion less dramatic but more informative, because each kind of uncertainty points to a different next step. The strongest objection came from another direction: finance officers argued that demand alone could not justify a service with uncertain long-term usage. It would have been easy to summarize that view briefly and dismiss it, but the reviewers instead asked what would follow if the objection were partly right. Some parts of the proposal survived unchanged; others required a smaller scale, a later deadline, or a clearer review threshold. This exercise mattered because a conclusion that can absorb a serious objection is generally stronger than one protected by ignoring it. The eventual decision reflected that narrower reasoning: the university approved a smaller pilot in two laboratories with predefined review criteria. What made the outcome useful was not only its content but its reversibility. The group specified what future evidence would justify expansion, revision, or withdrawal. In effect, the recommendation became a structured hypothesis about what should happen next rather than a declaration that debate had ended. This made implementation and later evaluation part of the same reasoning process. What the case ultimately demonstrates is that concession allows a writer to acknowledge a genuine weakness while showing why another consideration still carries greater weight. The quality of an advanced argument often depends on small linguistic distinctions: whether a source claims or demonstrates, whether a result may occur or is expected to occur, whether a limitation narrows scope or undermines validity, and whether a contrast deserves emphasis or only acknowledgement. These choices shape how readers understand responsibility and certainty long after they have forgotten the exact wording of the original evidence. In practical terms, this means arguing for a limited pilot while openly acknowledging cost and operational objections. The challenge is to produce language that survives both immediate use and later scrutiny: clear enough to guide action, qualified enough to remain accurate, and structured enough for another reader to reconstruct the reasoning. That combination of flexibility and accountability is more valuable than surface complexity.

| much as | مع أن | Use much as to concede a proposition before asserting a contrasting main point. |

| even granting | حتى مع التسليم بـ | + Even granting the cost estimates, a smaller pilot could still produce useful evidence. |
| concessive frame | إطار تنازلي | The unit uses “concessive frame” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |

## Comprehension
1. What decision did the academic planning committee need to make?
2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

- Listen for instances of complex argumentation and how the speakers integrate concessions to strengthen their positions, rather than weaken them.

## Transcript
Omar: Sara, thank you for carving out some time from what I know is an extraordinarily packed schedule. We really need to get to grips with this proposal for the extended evening access pilot, particularly discerning where the most compelling evidence truly lies.

Sara: Of course, Omar. It’s always a pleasure to chew over these thorny issues with you. To my mind, the unequivocal primary driver here stems from the longitudinal student surveys, which consistently highlight a profound demand among our final-year researchers who are juggling daytime placements. It’s hardly a mere anecdotal whim; it’s a robust data point.

Omar: I concur entirely on that front. Though it's a potent indicator, one must ask: is there any independent corroboration to bolster this, or are we, for all that, still resting our case predominantly on a single evidentiary strand?

Sara: It's an astute observation, and one I've anticipated. Indeed, there’s a second, albeit complementary, strand that gives it further heft: a recent internal audit revealed that two specific departments already have trained personnel on-site during a significant portion of the proposed evening access window. It strikes me that the convergence of these two points forms a rather formidable, if not entirely unassailable, case.

Omar: That certainly paints a more comprehensive picture. However, where do you see the most significant impedance, the argument that could most effectively throw a spanner in the works of a full-scale endorsement? What’s the strongest countervailing force?

Sara: Were I to distil it to its essence, the most salient limitation, which one simply cannot sweep under the rug, is the considerable financial outlay. What with the additional security, enhanced supervision protocols, and the inevitable hike in insurance premiums, the projected costs are far from negligible. It’s what tempers any overly enthusiastic generalization of the pilot's potential.

Omar: Ah, the perennial financial tightrope. Apropos of that, our finance officers posited a rather pointed counter-argument: that demand, however seemingly robust, could scarcely justify initiating a service whose long-term usage remains, in their estimation, somewhat conjectural. To what extent do you perceive this as fundamentally altering the thrust of our recommendation?

Sara: It’s a compelling point, no doubt. Yet, to my mind, it modifies the parameters and the scope of the recommendation rather than fundamentally changing its trajectory. What it absolutely necessitates is an explicit acknowledgement of this fiscal objection, confronting it head-on, rather than simply feigning ignorance or dismissing it as an inconvenient trifle.

Omar: So, putting aside the rhetoric for a moment, what pragmatic, actionable recommendation would you advocate as the immediate next step, given these competing exigencies?

Sara: My counsel would be to sanction a more circumscribed pilot program, perhaps confined to two specific laboratories, replete with clearly delineated, measurable review criteria. This approach allows us to move forward decisively, for all the uncertainties, without indulging in the pretense that all potential snags have miraculously vanished. It’s a pragmatic compromise, an artful dodger of outright commitment while still progressing.

Omar: A judicious path forward, indeed. And finally, Omar, in crafting the definitive statement for the final document, how best should we frame the overarching conclusion? What principle should underpin our articulation?

Sara: My conviction is that we must foreground the principle of considered concession throughout. It’s an invaluable rhetorical device. It enables us to unequivocally acknowledge a genuine, perhaps even unsettling, weakness or limitation in our proposal, whilst simultaneously elucidating precisely why another paramount consideration, or indeed a constellation of considerations, still ultimately tips the scales in its favour. That’s how we present a robust, yet transparent, argument.

Omar: Eloquently put, Sara. It sounds like we have a consensus on the strategic deployment of concession. Thank you.

Sara: My pleasure, Omar.

## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating arguing for a limited pilot while openly acknowledging cost and operational objections. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Advanced concession and contrast naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on arguing for a limited pilot while openly acknowledging cost and operational objections requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that student surveys showed strong demand among final-year researchers with daytime placements. In addition, two departments already had trained staff on site during part of the proposed evening period. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because additional security, supervision, and insurance costs would be significant. A credible objection is that finance officers argued that demand alone could not justify a service with uncertain long-term usage. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the university approved a smaller pilot in two laboratories with predefined review criteria. This conclusion remains open to revision because concession allows a writer to acknowledge a genuine weakness while showing why another consideration still carries greater weight. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using advanced concession and contrast where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on arguing for a limited pilot while openly acknowledging cost and operational objections. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that student surveys showed strong demand among final-year researchers with daytime placements. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that two departments already had trained staff on site during part of the proposed evening period. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? contents.title: Grammar: Ellipsis and substitution in connected discourse
contents.body:
## Why it matters
Ellipsis omits material that can be recovered from context; substitution replaces repeated material with forms such as one, ones, do so, or so. These resources make advanced discourse economical, but only when the omitted or substituted meaning remains unambiguous.

At C1, Ellipsis and substitution in connected discourse is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| verbal ellipsis | auxiliary retained; repeated verb phrase omitted | Some editors restored the words; others did not. |
| do substitution | do so = previously mentioned action | The team expanded only passages that needed it; they did so selectively. |
| nominal substitution | one/ones replaces count noun phrase | The shorter version was clearer than the original one. |
| clausal substitution | so/not replaces clause content | Will the context remain clear? I think so. |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ Some speakers repeated the full phrase, but most did not.
+ When expansion was necessary, the editor did so carefully.
+ The natural transcript was easier to read than the fully expanded one.
+ Will readers recover the omitted meaning? In most cases, I think so.
- The team did not restore every missing word simply because the transcript was written.
? Which auxiliary remains in “Some did, others didn’t”?
? What does one replace in “the original one”?
? When would ellipsis become unsafe?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Use ellipsis when grammar and context make the missing material easy to recover.
- Use do so for an action or process when repetition would be cumbersome; avoid it where ordinary do is more natural.
- Use one/ones for count nouns, not as a universal substitute for every noun phrase.
- Use so/not to substitute for clauses after verbs such as think, hope, suppose, and expect where idiomatic.
- Restore explicit wording when a text has been detached from the context that licensed the ellipsis.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~Some editors expanded the phrase; others expanded.~~ -> Some editors expanded the phrase; others did too. / others did not.
~~The team decided to revise the transcript and did it so.~~ -> The team decided to revise the transcript and did so.
~~This version is clearer than the original it.~~ -> This version is clearer than the original one.
~~Will it be clear? I think it so.~~ -> Will it be clear? I think so.

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of ellipsis & substitution, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

## Quick Recap
- Ellipsis omits recoverable material.
- Substitution avoids unnecessary repetition.
- Auxiliaries often license verbal ellipsis.
- One/ones replace count noun phrases.
- Context determines whether economy remains clear.

ابدأ دائمًا من المعنى المقصود، ثم حدّد الجزء الذي يتحكم في القاعدة، وبعد ذلك اختر الصيغة المناسبة. من المفيد قراءة الأمثلة بصوت مرتفع، ثم تغيير عنصر واحد فقط في كل مرة مثل الفاعل أو الزمن أو المكان أو درجة التأكد. هذه الطريقة تمنع الحفظ الآلي وتساعد على استخدام القاعدة في مواقف جديدة.

## الصيغة
| Focus | Form | Example |
| verbal ellipsis | auxiliary retained; repeated verb phrase omitted | Some editors restored the words; others did not. |
| do substitution | do so = previously mentioned action | The team expanded only passages that needed it; they did so selectively. |
| nominal substitution | one/ones replaces count noun phrase | The shorter version was clearer than the original one. |
| clausal substitution | so/not replaces clause content | Will the context remain clear? I think so. |

اقرأ الجدول كدليل لاتخاذ القرار. حدّد أولًا نوع المعنى أو الوظيفة، ثم اختر الصيغة المقابلة لها. إذا وُجد أكثر من تركيب ممكن نحويًا، فاختر التركيب الذي يعبّر بدقة أكبر عن المعنى المقصود في السياق. في المستويات الأعلى، انتبه أيضًا إلى السجل اللغوي، ودرجة الرسمية، وترتيب المعلومات، ومدى قوة الادعاء.

## أمثلة
+ Some speakers repeated the full phrase, but most did not.
+ When expansion was necessary, the editor did so carefully.
+ The natural transcript was easier to read than the fully expanded one.
+ Will readers recover the omitted meaning? In most cases, I think so.
- The team did not restore every missing word simply because the transcript was written.
? Which auxiliary remains in “Some did, others didn’t”?
? What does one replace in “the original one”?
? When would ellipsis become unsafe?

الأمثلة السابقة هي نماذج للاستخدام. لا يكفي أن تعرف أن الجملة صحيحة؛ حاول أن تشرح لماذا اختيرت هذه الصيغة وما الذي سيتغير لو استُخدمت صيغة أخرى قريبة منها. بعد ذلك أنشئ مثالًا جديدًا من عندك مع الحفاظ على نفس القاعدة وتغيير المفردات والسياق.

## متى نستخدمها؟
- استخدم **الحذف والاستبدال في الخطاب المترابط** عندما يحتاج المعنى في الجملة إلى الوظيفة التي تعرضها هذه الوحدة.
- اربط اختيار الصيغة بالسياق، ولا تعتمد على كلمة واحدة فقط كإشارة آلية.
- راجع الفاعل والزمن والأفعال المساعدة وترتيب الكلمات قبل إنهاء الجملة.
- في الكتابة، تأكد من أن القاعدة تخدم ترابط الفكرة ولا تجعل الجملة أعقد من اللازم.
- في التحدث، درّب نفسك على إنتاج الصيغة بسرعة من خلال أمثلة قصيرة ثم انتقل إلى إجابات أطول.

بعد التصحيح، أعد صياغة الجملة بدل الاكتفاء بقراءة الإجابة الصحيحة. اكتب أو قل فكرة ثانية بنفس القاعدة، لأن إعادة الاستخدام هي التي تثبت الفهم الحقيقي وتقلل الاعتماد على الأمثلة المحفوظة.

## أخطاء شائعة
~~Some editors expanded the phrase; others expanded.~~ -> Some editors expanded the phrase; others did too. / others did not.
~~The team decided to revise the transcript and did it so.~~ -> The team decided to revise the transcript and did so.
~~This version is clearer than the original it.~~ -> This version is clearer than the original one.
~~Will it be clear? I think it so.~~ -> Will it be clear? I think so.

عند حدوث خطأ، حدّد أولًا موضع المشكلة، ثم ارجع إلى الصيغة في الجدول، وأعد بناء الجملة خطوة بخطوة. بعد ذلك كوّن مثالًا جديدًا يغيّر الفاعل أو الزمن أو السياق. بهذه الطريقة يصبح التصحيح تدريبًا على القاعدة نفسها وليس مجرد حفظ للجملة الصحيحة.

## مراجعة سريعة
- افهم المعنى قبل اختيار الصيغة.
- راجع شكل القاعدة في الجدول ثم طبّقه في سياق حقيقي.
- قارن بين المثال الصحيح والخطأ الشائع لتعرف الفرق بدقة.
- استخدم القاعدة في جمل مثبتة ومنفية وأسئلة عندما يكون ذلك طبيعيًا.
- أعد استخدام القاعدة بمفردات جديدة حتى يصبح الاختيار تلقائيًا.

## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating editing spoken language into readable text without destroying natural cohesion and economy. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Ellipsis and substitution in connected discourse naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on editing spoken language into readable text without destroying natural cohesion and economy requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that speakers frequently omitted repeated auxiliaries, verbs, or noun phrases when the missing material was obvious from the previous turn. In addition, substitutes such as do so, one, ones, and so allowed participants to maintain cohesion without repeating full expressions. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because some omissions became difficult to interpret after excerpts were removed from their original conversational context. A credible objection is that a junior editor wanted to restore every omitted word in order to make the written transcript grammatically complete. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the team preserved natural ellipsis where reference remained clear and expanded only those passages that became ambiguous in isolation. This conclusion remains open to revision because economy is effective when the listener or reader can reliably recover the missing material from grammar and context. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using ellipsis and substitution in connected discourse where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

Omar: Well, Sara, what is undeniably significant is the demonstrable twofold increase in volunteer engagement, coupled with an outreach expansion into several previously unserved neighborhoods. This, I contend, is hardly anecdotal; it represents a quantifiable leap.
Sara: Agreed, that’s compelling. But what’s crucial now is discerning whether this data stands in splendid isolation, or if there’s corroborating evidence that bolsters its veracity. Are we dealing with a singular datum, however robust, or a multifaceted affirmation?
Omar: It is precisely that multifaceted affirmation which lends substantial weight to our claims. What we also have is independently commissioned feedback, describing the service not merely as 'satisfactory,' but as 'unquestionably reliable' and 'significantly more accessible' than its preceding iteration. I’d argue it's the confluence of these two independent strands that gives us a truly formidable foundation.
Sara: And what, then, is the elephant in the room? What constitutes the most potent caveat against letting our enthusiasm run unbridled, potentially veering into hyperbole? We need to ground this in sober reality.
Omar: The principal limitation, to put it mildly, is that while progress has been remarkable, it is not as if every single target demographic has been comprehensively reached. Furthermore, a non-negligible proportion of these improvements were contingent upon transitory funding, which fundamentally restricts the generalisability of our conclusions. This isn't merely a minor quibble; it's a structural constraint.
Sara: Indeed. Now, our campaign staff, bless their hearts, are advocating for what they term 'unapologetically dramatic' language. They posit that anything less might simply be lost in the din, attracting insufficient attention. Does this pragmatic consideration, however mercenary, not significantly alter the calculus of our final recommendation?
Omar: It certainly adds another layer of complexity to the calculus, that much is undeniable. But what it primarily impacts are the contextual conditions surrounding the recommendation, rather than fundamentally altering its core direction. To dismiss their concern would be churlish, even foolhardy; what we must do is acknowledge it explicitly, rather than pretending such strategic imperatives are somehow trivial.
Sara: So, integrating these various, sometimes conflicting, currents, what pragmatic outcome would you ultimately advocate for as the optimal way forward?
Omar: What I would wholeheartedly endorse is a presentation strategy that employs judicious emphasis on demonstrably verified achievements. What this entails is avoiding any superlatives that the evidentiary corpus simply cannot sustain. It offers a principled pathway forward, enabling us to make a definitive statement without succumbing to the illusion that all uncertainty has been magically expunged.
Sara: That sounds like a judicious balance. And for the formal record, the final document, how should we encapsulate this guiding philosophy?
Omar: For the overarching documentation, the leitmotif must be this: it is advanced emphasis that should invariably elevate the salience of our findings. What it must never do is transmute a robust, defensible claim into an unsupportable, inflated one. That distinction, to my mind, is paramount.
Sara: That's a crucial distinction, Omar. It's precisely this nuanced approach that will stand up to scrutiny.
Omar: Precisely. It is integrity that we must prioritise above all else.
Sara: Couldn't agree more. What we've discussed today provides a solid foundation.

## Key phrases
- what is undeniably significant
- the elephant in the room
- let our enthusiasm run unbridled
- a non-negligible proportion
- what it must never do is transmute

## Comprehension
1. What specific evidence does Omar initially present to advocate for a more enthusiastic tone in the presentation?
2. How does Sara challenge Omar’s initial evidence, and what kind of additional data does Omar then introduce to strengthen his position?
3. What is the fundamental restriction Omar identifies regarding the generalisability of the project's conclusions, despite its successes?
4. How does Omar differentiate the campaign staff’s desire for ‘dramatic language’ from its potential impact on the core recommendation?
5. According to Omar, what is the 'leitmotif' or guiding principle that should underpin the final document's philosophy regarding emphasis?

4. Omar states that it primarily impacts the contextual conditions surrounding the recommendation rather than altering its core direction, and that their concern must be acknowledged explicitly.

contents.title: Grammar: Emphasis with auxiliaries, degree and exclamative structures
contents.body:
## Why it matters
Advanced emphasis can be grammatical, lexical, prosodic, or structural. C1 users should know how do-support, so/such, what/how exclamatives, and contrastive auxiliary stress intensify a message while still preserving factual accuracy and genre appropriacy.

At C1, Emphasis with auxiliaries, degree and exclamative structures is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| emphatic do | do/does/did + base verb | The project did reach more neighborhoods than expected. |
| so...that | so + adjective/adverb + that-clause | Demand was so strong that the team added a second site. |
| such...that | such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that-clause | It was such a strong response that the plan was expanded. |
| exclamative | What + noun phrase! / How + adjective/adverb! | What a significant improvement the survey recorded! |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ The project did exceed its original participation target.
+ Demand was so strong that additional sessions were scheduled.
+ It was such a visible improvement that local media reported it.
+ What a remarkable increase in volunteer participation the team recorded!
- The presentation did not claim that every target group had been reached.
? Did the project actually meet the verified access target?
? How strong was the improvement relative to the original plan?
? When would emphatic do sound defensive rather than celebratory?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Use emphatic do when affirming a point that has been doubted, corrected, or contrasted.
- Use so + adjective/adverb and such + noun phrase with that-clauses to express degree and consequence.
- Use exclamatives sparingly in formal contexts; they are strongly marked.
- Let prosody carry some emphasis in speech rather than piling up intensifiers.
- Do not use grammatical emphasis to strengthen an evidential claim beyond what the data supports.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~The project did exceeded the target.~~ -> The project did exceed the target.
~~It was so successful project that funding increased.~~ -> It was such a successful project that funding increased.
~~Such strong was demand that sessions expanded.~~ -> So strong was demand that sessions expanded. / Demand was so strong that sessions expanded.
~~What the project was successful!~~ -> How successful the project was! / What a successful project it was!

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of emphasis, degree & exclamative patterns, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

Editing work should distinguish error from preference. First correct forms that are ungrammatical or that distort the intended meaning. Then consider whether a more idiomatic, concise, or audience-sensitive alternative would improve the text. This two-stage process protects accuracy while acknowledging that advanced English often allows multiple acceptable formulations with different rhetorical effects.

## Quick Recap
- Do + base verb can create contrastive emphasis.
- So modifies adjective/adverb; such introduces a noun phrase.
- Exclamatives are highly marked.
- Prosody matters in spoken emphasis.
- Emphasis should not distort evidential strength.

## لماذا هذه القاعدة مهمة؟
تركّز هذه الوحدة على **التوكيد بالأفعال المساعدة والدرجة وصيغ التعجب** داخل موضوع «التوكيد والدرجة وصيغ التعجب». الهدف ليس حفظ شكل القاعدة وحده، بل فهم العلاقة بين الصيغة والمعنى ثم استخدامها بصورة صحيحة في القراءة والكتابة والاستماع والتحدث. في مستوى C1.2 (متقدم)، يجب أن يلاحظ المتعلم ما الذي يحدد اختيار الصيغة: الفاعل، الزمن، درجة اليقين، العلاقة بين الأحداث، أو الغرض من الجملة.

ابدأ دائمًا من المعنى المقصود، ثم حدّد الجزء الذي يتحكم في القاعدة، وبعد ذلك اختر الصيغة المناسبة. من المفيد قراءة الأمثلة بصوت مرتفع، ثم تغيير عنصر واحد فقط في كل مرة مثل الفاعل أو الزمن أو المكان أو درجة التأكد. هذه الطريقة تمنع الحفظ الآلي وتساعد على استخدام القاعدة في مواقف جديدة.

## الصيغة
| Focus | Form | Example |
| emphatic do | do/does/did + base verb | The project did reach more neighborhoods than expected. |
| so...that | so + adjective/adverb + that-clause | Demand was so strong that the team added a second site. |
| such...that | such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that-clause | It was such a strong response that the plan was expanded. |
| exclamative | What + noun phrase! / How + adjective/adverb! | What a significant improvement the survey recorded! |

اقرأ الجدول كدليل لاتخاذ القرار. حدّد أولًا نوع المعنى أو الوظيفة، ثم اختر الصيغة المقابلة لها. إذا وُجد أكثر من تركيب ممكن نحويًا، فاختر التركيب الذي يعبّر بدقة أكبر عن المعنى المقصود في السياق. في المستويات الأعلى، انتبه أيضًا إلى السجل اللغوي، ودرجة الرسمية، وترتيب المعلومات، ومدى قوة الادعاء.

## أمثلة
+ The project did exceed its original participation target.
+ Demand was so strong that additional sessions were scheduled.
+ It was such a visible improvement that local media reported it.
+ What a remarkable increase in volunteer participation the team recorded!
- The presentation did not claim that every target group had been reached.
? Did the project actually meet the verified access target?
? How strong was the improvement relative to the original plan?
? When would emphatic do sound defensive rather than celebratory?

الأمثلة السابقة هي نماذج للاستخدام. لا يكفي أن تعرف أن الجملة صحيحة؛ حاول أن تشرح لماذا اختيرت هذه الصيغة وما الذي سيتغير لو استُخدمت صيغة أخرى قريبة منها. بعد ذلك أنشئ مثالًا جديدًا من عندك مع الحفاظ على نفس القاعدة وتغيير المفردات والسياق.

## متى نستخدمها؟
- استخدم **التوكيد بالأفعال المساعدة والدرجة وصيغ التعجب** عندما يحتاج المعنى في الجملة إلى الوظيفة التي تعرضها هذه الوحدة.
- اربط اختيار الصيغة بالسياق، ولا تعتمد على كلمة واحدة فقط كإشارة آلية.
- راجع الفاعل والزمن والأفعال المساعدة وترتيب الكلمات قبل إنهاء الجملة.
- في الكتابة، تأكد من أن القاعدة تخدم ترابط الفكرة ولا تجعل الجملة أعقد من اللازم.
- في التحدث، درّب نفسك على إنتاج الصيغة بسرعة من خلال أمثلة قصيرة ثم انتقل إلى إجابات أطول.

بعد التصحيح، أعد صياغة الجملة بدل الاكتفاء بقراءة الإجابة الصحيحة. اكتب أو قل فكرة ثانية بنفس القاعدة، لأن إعادة الاستخدام هي التي تثبت الفهم الحقيقي وتقلل الاعتماد على الأمثلة المحفوظة.

## أخطاء شائعة
~~The project did exceeded the target.~~ -> The project did exceed the target.
~~It was so successful project that funding increased.~~ -> It was such a successful project that funding increased.
~~Such strong was demand that sessions expanded.~~ -> So strong was demand that sessions expanded. / Demand was so strong that sessions expanded.
~~What the project was successful!~~ -> How successful the project was! / What a successful project it was!

عند حدوث خطأ، حدّد أولًا موضع المشكلة، ثم ارجع إلى الصيغة في الجدول، وأعد بناء الجملة خطوة بخطوة. بعد ذلك كوّن مثالًا جديدًا يغيّر الفاعل أو الزمن أو السياق. بهذه الطريقة يصبح التصحيح تدريبًا على القاعدة نفسها وليس مجرد حفظ للجملة الصحيحة.

## مراجعة سريعة
- افهم المعنى قبل اختيار الصيغة.
- راجع شكل القاعدة في الجدول ثم طبّقه في سياق حقيقي.
- قارن بين المثال الصحيح والخطأ الشائع لتعرف الفرق بدقة.
- استخدم القاعدة في جمل مثبتة ومنفية وأسئلة عندما يكون ذلك طبيعيًا.
- أعد استخدام القاعدة بمفردات جديدة حتى يصبح الاختيار تلقائيًا.

## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating presenting strong results persuasively while avoiding unsupported exaggeration. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Emphasis with auxiliaries, degree and exclamative structures naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on presenting strong results persuasively while avoiding unsupported exaggeration requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that volunteer participation doubled and the programme reached more neighborhoods than originally planned. In addition, independent feedback described the service as reliable and easier to access than the previous arrangement. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because the project had not reached every target group and some improvements depended on temporary funding. A credible objection is that campaign staff preferred highly dramatic language because they feared a cautious message would attract less attention. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the final presentation used emphasis on verified achievements but avoided superlatives that the evidence could not support. This conclusion remains open to revision because advanced emphasis should increase salience without changing a defensible claim into an inflated one. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using emphasis with auxiliaries, degree and exclamative structures where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on presenting strong results persuasively while avoiding unsupported exaggeration. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that volunteer participation doubled and the programme reached more neighborhoods than originally planned. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that independent feedback described the service as reliable and easier to access than the previous arrangement. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? Speaker B: Not quite, because the project had not reached every target group and some improvements depended on temporary funding. Speaker A: Some colleagues would say that campaign staff preferred highly dramatic language because they feared a cautious message would attract less attention. Speaker B: That is a serious objection. I would acknowledge it explicitly, then explain why the final presentation used emphasis on verified achievements but avoided superlatives that the evidence could not support still seems proportionate. Speaker A: So the conclusion is conditional rather than weak. Speaker B: Exactly. Advanced emphasis should increase salience without changing a defensible claim into an inflated one. The wording should communicate that distinction clearly.

Draft a 220–280 word formal proposal, report, or critical review related to presenting strong results persuasively while avoiding unsupported exaggeration. Control register, paragraph cohesion, and information focus.

Purpose: This document evaluates presenting strong results persuasively while avoiding unsupported exaggeration. Evidence: Volunteer participation doubled and the programme reached more neighborhoods than originally planned. A second relevant consideration is that independent feedback described the service as reliable and easier to access than the previous arrangement. ## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about impersonal reporting passives require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
Within an economic policy unit drafting a briefing before official statistics are released, a seemingly straightforward question became an exercise in judgment rather than procedure. The central responsibility belonged to the senior economist, Dalia Mourad. The decision was how to refer to market expectations that have not yet been confirmed by published data. The issue mattered because an early decision would shape what colleagues, stakeholders, and later reviewers treated as the working interpretation. A premature conclusion could create momentum that was difficult to reverse, while excessive caution could delay a useful response. The group therefore treated the wording of the decision as part of the decision itself: what it said needed to reflect not only preference, but what the available information could actually support. Two strands of evidence carried most weight. First, several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. Second, business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. Their convergence made it difficult to dismiss the issue as a one-off impression, yet the group resisted the easy leap from consistency to certainty. The strands did not necessarily measure the same construct, and neither automatically established a single causal explanation. Their real value lay in the pattern they formed and in the sharper questions that pattern allowed reviewers to ask. The main caveat was substantial: the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. A limitation of this kind does not necessarily invalidate the underlying evidence; it changes what the evidence is entitled to support. The reviewers therefore replaced the crude question ‘Is the evidence good or bad?’ with a more useful one: ‘What is this evidence good enough to show?’ That distinction matters whenever a reliable dataset is narrow, a credible witness has only partial access, or a coherent model remains sensitive to assumptions that are open to challenge. A credible counter-position also had to be represented: one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. The group did not include this view as a ceremonial concession before returning to its preferred answer. Members tested whether the objection changed the interpretation of the evidence, the cost of acting, or the cost of waiting. In several parts of the discussion, the counterargument narrowed the wording and sharpened the conditions attached to the recommendation. That made the final position more defensible because the strongest alternative explanation had been answered rather than caricatured. The practical outcome was measured rather than dramatic: the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. Just as important, the decision contained a theory of revision. If later evidence challenged the assumptions, the organization would have a defined reason to reconsider instead of defending the earlier position merely for consistency. Colleagues could also see which part of the conclusion rested on direct evidence, which part was inferential, and which part represented a judgment about acceptable risk. That transparency reduced the chance that a cautious claim would later be remembered as a categorical promise. The wider lesson is that reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. Language contributes directly to that discipline. A reporting verb can imply endorsement or distance; a conditional can distinguish a real possibility from a remote hypothetical; a focusing structure can correct a mistaken assumption; and a nominal phrase can either package a familiar concept efficiently or conceal the agent who acted. Complexity is therefore not the goal. The relevant question is which formulation makes the logic, stance, and information structure most accurate for the audience and genre. For anyone facing a similar problem, the practical task is drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. A strong response keeps the distinctions that matter, acknowledges uncertainty without becoming evasive, and remains readable enough for another person to act on. The result is not merely a more advanced piece of English. It is a better record of how a decision was reached and what would justify changing it.

## Key words
| Word | Meaning | Example |
| is thought to | يُعتقد أنه | The briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to. |
| is understood to | يُفهم أنه | The unit uses “is understood to” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| is estimated to | يُقدَّر أنه | The unit uses “is estimated to” to express a precise relationship involving stance, reference, logic, or discourse organization. |
| impersonal passive | مبني للمجهول غير شخصي | Do not use an impersonal passive to disguise weak evidence as institutional consensus. |
| source-neutral | محايد تجاه المصدر | The team discussed the source-neutral because it affected how the evidence and final decision should be interpreted. |

## Comprehension
1. What decision did the senior economist, Dalia Mourad need to make?
2. What was one important strand of evidence?
3. What second strand of evidence supported the discussion?
4. What was the main limitation?
5. What counter-position had to be considered?
6. What practical outcome was reached?

## Answers
1. how to refer to market expectations that have not yet been confirmed by published data
2. several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter
3. business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized
4. the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters
5. one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view
6. the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators

contents.body:
## Why it matters
Reporting passives allow writers to attribute beliefs, expectations, estimates, and reports without always foregrounding the source. They are common in formal genres, but they vary in time reference and evidential force. C1 users should preserve the distinction between what is known, expected, alleged, and estimated.

At C1, Impersonal and personal reporting passives is best treated as a discourse choice rather than an isolated rule. Learners should be able to select the structure according to emphasis, stance, information flow, and register, while retaining reliable control of form. The same proposition can often be expressed in several grammatically possible ways; advanced competence lies in choosing the version that best serves the communicative purpose.

## Form
| Focus | Form | Example |
| impersonal it | It + be + past participle + that-clause | It is expected that inflation will fall modestly. |
| personal reporting passive | subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive | Inflation is expected to fall modestly. |
| prior event | subject + be + past participle + to have + past participle | Costs are believed to have stabilized last quarter. |
| ongoing state/action | subject + be + past participle + to be + -ing/adjective | Demand is thought to be weakening gradually. |

Contrastive noticing should include near-equivalent alternatives. Ask what changes when the sentence is made more personal or impersonal, more categorical or more tentative, more neutral or more rhetorically marked. Learners should justify their selection in terms of meaning and context, not merely identify a memorized pattern.

## Examples
+ Inflation is expected to fall modestly during the next quarter.
+ It is understood that official figures will be released next week.
+ Energy costs are believed to have stabilized recently.
+ Demand is thought to be weakening in several sectors.
- The forecast is not known to be certain simply because many analysts share it.

? Who exactly is the source in an impersonal reporting passive?
? How should the wording change if the claim is only alleged?

Production practice should move quickly from sentence-level control to connected discourse. A useful sequence is reformulation, expansion, and register shift: first correct or transform a sentence; then embed it in a short argument or narrative; finally rewrite the same idea for a different audience. This reveals whether the grammar remains stable when lexical and pragmatic demands increase.

## Use it / When to use
- Use reporting passives to summarize attributed expectations or beliefs in formal prose.
- Use to have + past participle when the reported event precedes the reporting reference point.
- Choose the reporting participle carefully: expected, believed, reported, alleged, estimated, and known are not interchangeable.
- Name the source when source identity is important to evaluating credibility.
- Do not use an impersonal passive to disguise weak evidence as institutional consensus.

Feedback at this level should address appropriacy as well as grammaticality. A sentence may be formally correct but too emphatic, too vague, too conversational, or unnecessarily dense for the situation. Encourage learners to test alternatives and explain which one creates the intended focus, interpersonal effect, or degree of commitment.

## Common Mistakes
~~Inflation is expected that it will fall.~~ -> Inflation is expected to fall. / It is expected that inflation will fall.
~~Costs are believed to stabilize last quarter.~~ -> Costs are believed to have stabilized last quarter.
~~It is expected inflation to fall.~~ -> It is expected that inflation will fall.
~~The figure is known to maybe fall.~~ -> The figure is expected to fall. / It is possible that the figure will fall.

A useful final check is to ask whether the form changes the proposition, the degree of commitment, the information focus, or merely the style. Advanced accuracy includes knowing when a simpler structure would communicate the idea more efficiently.


In the context of impersonal reporting passives, learners should practise the target structure with lexical material that is sufficiently demanding to make the grammatical choice meaningful. Advanced control is often tested when several pressures operate at once: the speaker must maintain reference, signal stance, manage clause relationships, and preserve an appropriate register. Tasks should therefore include short stretches of connected language rather than a long sequence of decontextualized transformations.

Corpus-informed teaching at advanced levels also benefits from attention to distribution and conventionality. A construction may be theoretically possible but uncommon in the relevant genre, while another may be strongly associated with formal analysis, spoken disagreement, narrative emphasis, or institutional writing. Learners do not need to memorize frequency tables, but they should notice recurring phraseological patterns and the company that grammatical forms tend to keep.

## Quick Recap
- Two main patterns: it-passive and personal passive.
- Use perfect infinitive for prior events.
- Reporting participles differ in stance.
- Source backgrounding does not remove evidential responsibility.
- Name sources when credibility matters.

ابدأ دائمًا من المعنى المقصود، ثم حدّد الجزء الذي يتحكم في القاعدة، وبعد ذلك اختر الصيغة المناسبة. من المفيد قراءة الأمثلة بصوت مرتفع، ثم تغيير عنصر واحد فقط في كل مرة مثل الفاعل أو الزمن أو المكان أو درجة التأكد. هذه الطريقة تمنع الحفظ الآلي وتساعد على استخدام القاعدة في مواقف جديدة.

## الصيغة
| Focus | Form | Example |
| impersonal it | It + be + past participle + that-clause | It is expected that inflation will fall modestly. |
| personal reporting passive | subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive | Inflation is expected to fall modestly. |
| prior event | subject + be + past participle + to have + past participle | Costs are believed to have stabilized last quarter. |
| ongoing state/action | subject + be + past participle + to be + -ing/adjective | Demand is thought to be weakening gradually. |

اقرأ الجدول كدليل لاتخاذ القرار. حدّد أولًا نوع المعنى أو الوظيفة، ثم اختر الصيغة المقابلة لها. إذا وُجد أكثر من تركيب ممكن نحويًا، فاختر التركيب الذي يعبّر بدقة أكبر عن المعنى المقصود في السياق. في المستويات الأعلى، انتبه أيضًا إلى السجل اللغوي، ودرجة الرسمية، وترتيب المعلومات، ومدى قوة الادعاء.

## أمثلة
+ Inflation is expected to fall modestly during the next quarter.
+ It is understood that official figures will be released next week.
+ Energy costs are believed to have stabilized recently.
+ Demand is thought to be weakening in several sectors.
- The forecast is not known to be certain simply because many analysts share it.
? Which form would you use for an earlier event: to fall or to have fallen?
? Who exactly is the source in an impersonal reporting passive?
? How should the wording change if the claim is only alleged?

الأمثلة السابقة هي نماذج للاستخدام. لا يكفي أن تعرف أن الجملة صحيحة؛ حاول أن تشرح لماذا اختيرت هذه الصيغة وما الذي سيتغير لو استُخدمت صيغة أخرى قريبة منها. بعد ذلك أنشئ مثالًا جديدًا من عندك مع الحفاظ على نفس القاعدة وتغيير المفردات والسياق.

## متى نستخدمها؟
- استخدم **المبني للمجهول غير الشخصي والشخصي في النقل** عندما يحتاج المعنى في الجملة إلى الوظيفة التي تعرضها هذه الوحدة.
- اربط اختيار الصيغة بالسياق، ولا تعتمد على كلمة واحدة فقط كإشارة آلية.
- راجع الفاعل والزمن والأفعال المساعدة وترتيب الكلمات قبل إنهاء الجملة.
- في الكتابة، تأكد من أن القاعدة تخدم ترابط الفكرة ولا تجعل الجملة أعقد من اللازم.
- في التحدث، درّب نفسك على إنتاج الصيغة بسرعة من خلال أمثلة قصيرة ثم انتقل إلى إجابات أطول.

بعد التصحيح، أعد صياغة الجملة بدل الاكتفاء بقراءة الإجابة الصحيحة. اكتب أو قل فكرة ثانية بنفس القاعدة، لأن إعادة الاستخدام هي التي تثبت الفهم الحقيقي وتقلل الاعتماد على الأمثلة المحفوظة.

## أخطاء شائعة
~~Inflation is expected that it will fall.~~ -> Inflation is expected to fall. / It is expected that inflation will fall.
~~Costs are believed to stabilize last quarter.~~ -> Costs are believed to have stabilized last quarter.
~~It is expected inflation to fall.~~ -> It is expected that inflation will fall.
~~The figure is known to maybe fall.~~ -> The figure is expected to fall. / It is possible that the figure will fall.

عند حدوث خطأ، حدّد أولًا موضع المشكلة، ثم ارجع إلى الصيغة في الجدول، وأعد بناء الجملة خطوة بخطوة. بعد ذلك كوّن مثالًا جديدًا يغيّر الفاعل أو الزمن أو السياق. بهذه الطريقة يصبح التصحيح تدريبًا على القاعدة نفسها وليس مجرد حفظ للجملة الصحيحة.

## مراجعة سريعة
- افهم المعنى قبل اختيار الصيغة.
- راجع شكل القاعدة في الجدول ثم طبّقه في سياق حقيقي.
- قارن بين المثال الصحيح والخطأ الشائع لتعرف الفرق بدقة.
- استخدم القاعدة في جمل مثبتة ومنفية وأسئلة عندما يكون ذلك طبيعيًا.
- أعد استخدام القاعدة بمفردات جديدة حتى يصبح الاختيار تلقائيًا.

## Task 1
Write 240–300 words evaluating drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Qualify at least two claims, address a plausible counterargument, and use Impersonal and personal reporting passives naturally rather than mechanically.

## Model answer
A defensible position on drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact requires more than a simple preference. The strongest case for action is that several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. In addition, business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. These points are meaningful, but they should not be treated as unlimited proof because the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. A credible objection is that one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. That objection deserves a direct response rather than a token concession: it may alter the scale, timing, or conditions of action even if it does not reverse the overall direction. In my view, the case outcome provides the most proportionate model for action: the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. This conclusion remains open to revision because reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. The language of the recommendation should make that logic visible, using impersonal and personal reporting passives where it clarifies stance, focus, time relationship, or information structure rather than simply making the prose look more complex.

## Task 2
Give a 4-minute seminar-style response on drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Synthesize two perspectives, signal your degree of certainty, and reformulate one point for clarity.

## Model answer
Speaker A: I think the first point we should establish is that several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. Speaker B: Agreed, and I would add that business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. Speaker A: Does that justify the strongest possible conclusion? Speaker B: Not quite, because the official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. Speaker A: Some colleagues would say that one drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. Speaker B: That is a serious objection. I would acknowledge it explicitly, then explain why the briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators still seems proportionate. Speaker A: So the conclusion is conditional rather than weak. Speaker B: Exactly. Reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. The wording should communicate that distinction clearly.

## Task 3
Draft a 220–280 word formal proposal, report, or critical review related to drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Control register, paragraph cohesion, and information focus.

## Model answer
Purpose: This document evaluates drafting a professional briefing that reports a broad expectation without presenting it as established fact. Evidence: Several independent analysts expected inflation to fall modestly during the next quarter. A second relevant consideration is that business surveys also suggested that transport and energy costs had stabilized. Limitation: The official index had not been released and survey expectations had been wrong in previous quarters. Counter-position: One drafter proposed stating directly that inflation would fall because that was the dominant market view. Recommendation: The briefing used forms such as is expected to and is thought to while separating forecasts from confirmed indicators. Rationale: Reporting passives can create useful distance, but they do not remove the need to identify the evidential status of a claim. The proposed wording should remain concise, but it should preserve the distinction between observation, inference, and judgment so that later readers can see why the recommendation was reasonable and what evidence would justify revising it.

contents.title: Reading: When compact technical labels become hard to process
contents.body:
## Before you read
- Which parts of a decision about complex noun phrases require evidence, and which require judgment?
- What would make a conclusion sound too strong for the evidence supporting it?
- As you read, identify one direct observation, one inference, and one practical judgment.

## Text
The case developed within an engineering firm revising a safety manual for mixed specialist and non-specialist users. Responsibility for the judgment rested with the documentation lead, Tarek Shalaby. The decision concerned which dense noun phrases should be kept as technical labels and which should be unpacked into clauses. None of the available positions was absurd, which was precisely why the discussion demanded care. Each option highlighted a different risk: acting too quickly, waiting too long, or communicating a degree of certainty that the evidence did not warrant. Instead of asking which position sounded most confident, participants separated what could be observed directly from what had to be inferred and from what depended on a value judgment about acceptable consequences.
